find: Short identification questions about theatre roles (1 or 2 marks) reward precise use of the correct role name. Write “lighting designer”, not “the person in charge of lights”. For 4-mark questions about roles, name the role, describe one day-to-day activity, and link it to its contribution to the audience’s experience — those are three distinct marks in a short answer. For longer staging questions (12 or 20 marks), you must write from a clearly identified role: “as a set designer” or “as a lighting designer”. Switching between roles mid-answer without flagging it blurs your credit. The most common error in role-based questions is writing about what the character feels rather than what the named specialist does to communicate that feeling to the audience. The audience can only see what the performers and designers give them — keep your answer on the craft, not the plot.

In a question written from a named role, explain that specialist’s practical choices and their effect on the audience. Keep the answer on the craft, not the plot.

find: The spec identifies nine vocal elements. The seven most frequently tested are: pitch (how high or low the voice sounds), pace (how fast or slow the performer speaks), pause (deliberate silence — one of the most powerful tools in a performer’s kit), volume (how loud or soft), accent (regional or national speech pattern, which communicates class, background and belonging), intonation (the rise and fall of pitch within a phrase, which signals questions, sarcasm, or certainty), and phrasing (how the performer breaks a line into units of meaning, which controls where the emphasis falls and what the audience understands).

find: For performer interpretation questions (8 marks), you must provide both a vocal AND a physical choice, and both must be specific and anchored to a named moment. “I would say it angrily” has no mark-scheme credit. “I would raise my pitch and quicken my pace for the accusation, then drop to a near-whisper for the final line, while standing in complete stillness with my fists clenched at my sides” names vocal skill (pitch, pace, volume) and physical skill (stillness, gesture) and gives enough detail to be awarded Mastering marks. For 12-mark intentions questions, connect the performer choices to what the playwright intends the audience to understand or feel at that moment — the craft choices are the evidence; the intention is the analysis. For 20-mark extended responses, you must address both performer and designer choices — a 20-mark answer that only discusses performance will be capped at the Developing band.
replace: When a question asks you to write as a performer, make specific vocal or physical choices and anchor them to the named moment. “I would say it angrily” is too vague. “I would raise my pitch and quicken my pace for the accusation, then drop to a near-whisper for the final line, while standing in complete stillness with my fists clenched at my sides” names vocal skill (pitch, pace, volume) and physical skill (stillness, gesture). When explaining intentions, connect the performer’s choices to what the playwright wants the audience to understand or feel at that moment.
